newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-India sees end of colonialism in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-India sees end of colonialism in Hong Kong.

text.p: For many Indians, the transformation of Hong Kong from a British colony to part of mainland China is the final chapter in the demise of colonial rule.
The difference is that Hong Kong's handover at midnight on June 30 will be free of the suffering, anguish and bloodshed that marked India's independence movement.

Once known as the "The Jewel in the Crown", India gained freedom from British rule on August 15, 1947 after years of struggle, rancour and devastation. Fifty years later Hong Kong is being peacefully handed over to China.

"It is a difference of 50 years. Hong Kong's handover is going on so smoothly that there is not one refugee there and there is no unhappiness," said Sumitra Gandhi Kulkarni, the 67-year-old granddaughter of Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi.

Her grandfather was called "Mahatma" or "great soul" for his role in leading India to freedom. Many Indians credit him with the downfall of colonialism all over the world. Kulkarni said Hong Kong's handover differs sharply from the huge upheaval triggered by independence on the Indian subcontinent.

She was referring to the so-called Partition which carved out West and East Pakistan on either side of a monolithic India. Hundreds of thousands of Hindus, Moslems and Sikhs died in frenzied mob violence as the British-drawn borders were enforced.
Ironically, it is the estimated 28,000 Hong Kong residents of Indian origin who feel most threatened by the peaceful handover, because of fears of becoming stateless after the event.
Some Indian residents hold limited British National Overseas (BNO) passports which give them no right to live in Britain.
Britain has promised full passports to up to 8,000 of this group, but Indian consulate officials in Hong Kong say India has revoked the citizenship of people holding BNO's.
CONTRASTING STYLES
Kulkarni told Reuters that when her grandfather started his non-violent struggle for independence he opted for years of suffering, but things had changed vastly since then.

"Over the years things have improved and much less sacrifice has been demanded by the colonial powers in releasing their erstwhile colonies and the last such example is that of Hong Kong," Kulkarni said. Mahatma Gandhi's great-grandson, 38-year-old Tushar Gandhi, said that for him the handover of Hong Kong stirred little emotion.
"Sentimentally I am unmoved. There was no struggle. The British are giving it up because the treaty is coming to an end," Tushar said in a telephone interview from Bombay.

India underwent pain to gain freedom from the British, whereas the eminence of Hong Kong as a trade capital of the Far East was built up by the British and it was not colonised disregarding people's wishes, Gandhi said.
"Here it is a case of a tenant moving out at the end of the tenancy," said Tushar.
Noted Indian historian Ravinder Kumar noted that Hong Kong was being left by its colonial rulers in a much stronger position.
"If India was dominated by the British for two centuries why did they not leave India at the same level of prosperity as they have left Hong Kong?" he said.

Kumar, the director of the Nehru Memorial Museum and Library, said the process of shaking off colonial rulers was given impetus with the emergence of India as an independent state in 1947. Hong Kong's handover was a culmination of that process.
"It is the end of an era in human history which meant anguish and devastation for the people of Asia and Africa," Kumar said.
France, Spain and the United States all gave up colonies in the period since the late 1940's.
Kumar said the 19th and 20th centuries belonged to Europe and North America but the 21st would be much more of an Asian and African century, he said.
"The end of colonialism is not an end of the world as it is. It is the commencement of a new process," Kumar said.
Kumar said in Hong Kong's case it was a question of absorbing a very dynamic financial economy into a larger planned economy. "One would watch with interest how this absorption takes place."
LEARNING FROM EXPERIENCE

Kumar said that until 1947 there was no precedent in human history of a peaceful process of decolonisation. He said he felt Britain, in handling India's independence, acquired certain political and negotiating skills which were put to great use in later years.
"In the years that followed August 15, 1947 one sees clearly the manner in which what the British learnt...was put to very effective use in Sri Lanka and African colonies," Kumar said.

Kumar said the process of decolonisation was difficult in countries with a substantial white settlement. In Hong Kong there was a substantial European population but not a settled population like in Algeria or Kenya, he said.
"The triumph of 1947 is the triumph of Gandhian politics but the political culture of Britain was also part of it," he said.
He said had Gandhi been alive today his concerns would have been of a very different nature.
"His concern would have been what is the quality of moral and social poise that Hong Kong has created for itself with all its material abundance".
"That particular aspect of Hong Kong society would have worried him and legitimately so," Kumar said.
